plain: The registration form a company files with the SEC before selling shares to the public for the first time. It contains the prospectus: the business description, risks, audited financials and ownership.
The first public version of the prospectus, before the price is set. It is nicknamed a red herring after the red warning legend once printed on its cover. The price and share counts are left blank.
Anthropic's single biggest cost line: renting and leasing the chips, servers, power and data centers used both to train new models and to answer customers' requests.
A loan that turns into shares instead of being repaid in cash, usually at a price agreed in advance. Amazon lent Anthropic billions this way between 2023 and 2025.
When an IOU that converts into shares becomes worth more because the company's valuation rose, accounting rules make the company record the increase as a loss. No cash changes hands.

A critic's term for deals where a supplier invests in or lends to a customer, and the customer spends the money back with the supplier. It can make both sides' growth look bigger than outside demand alone would.
A supplier lending money or extending credit so a customer can buy its products. It is common and legitimate, but it concentrates risk if the customer stumbles.
An independent trust, holding a single Class T share with no economic value, that elects four of Anthropic's seven directors. Its trustees may not own Anthropic stock.
A contract where the buyer pays for a minimum amount whether or not it uses it. Several of Anthropic's compute deals work this way, with cash "true-ups" for any shortfall.
A promise by existing shareholders not to sell for a period after the IPO, so the market isn't flooded with stock. Anthropic's releases come in many small steps instead of one date.
GAAP is the official US accounting rulebook, and audited figures follow it. "Adjusted" or non-GAAP figures are the company's own versions that leave out items such as stock-based pay.
Paying employees in shares or options instead of cash. It doesn't use cash, but it dilutes shareholders, so many analysts treat it as a real cost.
When a company issues new shares, each existing share owns a smaller slice of the company.
Share price times the number of shares: what the stock market says the whole company is worth.
Share price divided by profit per share. A P/E of 30 means investors pay $30 for every $1 of annual profit.
Market value divided by annual revenue. It's used for companies that don't yet make steady profits.
A recent short period of revenue scaled up to a year, for example one month times twelve. It flatters fast-growing companies and is not an audited number.
The total for the most recent twelve months, whatever the fiscal calendar.

How much this year's revenue from last year's customers compares with what they paid a year ago. Anthropic's definition counts any customer that paid at least $1, which inflates the figure against a tiny base.

Amazon, Google and Microsoft resell Claude through their own cloud platforms. They collect the money, keep a fee, and pass the rest to Anthropic. These sales were 48% of revenue in the first half of 2026.

Booking the full price a customer pays (gross) versus only the part the company keeps after a reseller's cut (net). Anthropic books cloud-marketplace sales gross and counts the cloud's fee as an expense.

A company legally required to balance shareholders' financial interests against a stated public purpose. Anthropic's purpose is "the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."
A Nasdaq status for companies where one person or group controls board elections. It lets the company skip some independence rules for board committees.
Different classes of stock with different voting rights, so insiders can control votes while selling economic ownership to the public. Alphabet and Meta use simpler versions.
A pre-agreed facility under which a partner will lend or invest more money later, usually when conditions are met. Anthropic has undrawn facilities with Google, Amazon and Broadcom.
Interest paid by adding to the loan balance instead of in cash. Broadcom's $42B facility accrues 9% this way.
Volume-weighted average price: the average price a stock traded at over a period, weighted by how many shares changed hands. Several partner deals convert into stock at the 30-day VWAP.
A lease that works economically like buying with a loan. The asset and the debt both sit on the balance sheet. Anthropic's Broadcom chip leases are treated this way.
Revenue customers have contractually committed to that hasn't been delivered yet. Anthropic's was $10.8B at June 30, 2026, small next to its revenue because most usage is pay-as-you-go.
An offer to buy shares from existing holders, often employees, at a set price before a company is public.
New Nasdaq rules let a very large new listing join the Nasdaq-100 within weeks instead of waiting a season, which forces index funds to buy.
AI that does tasks rather than just answering questions. It plans steps and uses software tools to carry out a goal for you.
Specialized computer chips (such as GPUs or TPUs) that run AI math far faster and more cheaply than ordinary processors.
A doorway that lets other companies’ software send requests to Claude and get answers back automatically, without a human typing into a chat window.
Using today’s Claude to help build tomorrow’s Claude, for example by writing code and running experiments. Anthropic argues this speeds up progress over time.
Software and research tricks that get more AI capability out of the same number of chips, like a car engine getting more miles per gallon.
Anthropic’s method of teaching Claude to behave well by giving it a written rulebook of values and having it check and revise its own answers against those rules.
The most advanced AI models available at any given moment.
Running a finished AI model to answer a request. It is the ‘serving customers’ part of AI costs, as opposed to building (training) the model.
Taking an AI model apart, like reverse-engineering a machine, to find which internal parts cause which behaviors, including hidden unsafe ones.
The billions of numbers that make up a trained AI model. They are the model itself and the company’s crown-jewel asset.
AI models whose core files are given away publicly so anyone can run or modify them. Some competitors take this approach.
Pay-as-you-go pricing: customers are billed for how much AI work they use, like a utility bill. It made up about 80% of revenue in H1 2026 (F-26).
The ‘finishing school’ stage that turns a raw model into a helpful, safe assistant good at real tasks like coding.
The first, most compute-hungry training stage, where the model reads vast amounts of text and learns general knowledge by guessing the next word.
A snapshot of the last four weeks’ revenue scaled up to a full year. It is a speed reading, not actual annual revenue, and can misstate the year if usage spikes or drops.
The small chunks (roughly word fragments) that AI reads and writes. AI usage is measured and priced per token, like minutes on a phone plan.
Anthropic’s most powerful model. The public version (Fable) has extra safety limits on sensitive topics, while vetted security and science organizations get a less restricted version (Mythos).
A limited-access program that gave Anthropic’s most capable model first to vetted cybersecurity defenders, because it is very good at finding software security holes.
An AI programmer that can carry out whole software tasks, not just suggest lines of code.
Claude Code’s approach applied to office work: you describe a task in plain language and it does the clicking, drafting and organizing for you.
A common ‘plug’ standard that lets AI assistants connect to company data and software, like a USB port for AI. Anthropic created it and gave it to an open-source foundation.
A privacy option where Anthropic deletes customer requests and answers right after processing them.
Instead of only renting computing power from cloud companies, Anthropic leases its own chips and data center space, run for it by partners.
Brand families of AI chips. GPUs come from NVIDIA and AMD; TPUs are Google’s own chips; Trainium is Amazon’s own chip.
Anthropic’s public rulebook for testing each new model for dangerous abilities and adding safeguards, or delaying release, before it ships.
Making sure the AI actually does what people want. ‘Misaligned’ AI pursues the wrong goals or takes actions nobody asked for.
AI that builds better AI, which builds even better AI, and so on. This could speed progress dramatically and is treated as a safety risk.
Anthropic’s strategy of making safety a competitive selling point so rivals feel pressure to match it.

term: supply-chain risk designation (10 U.S.C. § 3252 / FASCSA Section 4713)
plain: A U.S. military label that can bar defense contractors from doing business with Anthropic. Anthropic is fighting it in court with mixed results so far.
A $1.5 billion payment to settle authors’ claims that their books were copied to train Claude.
An early-stage investment contract that turns into shares later.

term: redeemable convertible preferred stock / Preferred Stock Conversion
plain: Special shares sold to venture and strategic investors. At the IPO they turn into ordinary shares.
Promised employee shares that vest over time. Many vest at the IPO, and some shares are held back to pay employees’ taxes.

term: Class F common stock / Founder LLC
plain: A special share that gives the founders together a majority of shareholder votes, but no claim on profits.

term: Class A / Class N / Class E common stock
plain: Different share types: A is what the public buys; N is economically identical but non-voting (mostly for partners like big tech investors); E gives employees a narrow say.

term: Anthropic Public Benefit Fund / Initial Public Benefit Issuance / Public Benefit Issuances
plain: Anthropic set aside 5% of its shares for public-good causes, with more to come if the stock rises. Note this dilutes other shareholders.
Anthropic doubles employees’ charitable stock donations with newly issued shares.
